content:
Quick answer: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.

Overview

Reasonable adjustments are a legal entitlement, not a favour.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews consistently highlight the importance of early intervention and ongoing management in arthritis care. While there's no single cure, research from numerous randomised trials shows that a combination of pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments can significantly reduce pain, improve function, and enhance quality of life for people living with various forms of arthritis.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies reinforce this, recommending a personalised approach. This includes careful diagnosis, medication tailored to the individual's condition and symptoms, and a strong emphasis on self-management strategies. Evidence also points to the benefits of regular physical activity adapted to individual capabilities, education about the condition, and psychological support where needed.

The effectiveness of 'reasonable adjustments' in the workplace, for instance, is supported by evidence demonstrating that flexible working conditions and ergonomic adaptations can reduce absenteeism, improve productivity, and help retain experienced employees living with long-term health conditions. This isn't just about compliance; it's about creating a sustainable, inclusive work environment.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Hoping pain will resolve on its own can delay effective treatment. *Fix: See a doctor for persistent joint pain or swelling. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing through pain can lead to flare-ups and setbacks. *Fix: Pace yourself and listen to your body, even when you feel well. Stopping medication too soon: Feeling better often means the medication is working, not that you no longer need it. *Fix: Always discuss medication changes with your doctor. Neglecting regular movement: Fear of pain can lead to inactivity, worsening stiffness and weakness. *Fix: Engage in gentle, low-impact exercise regularly. Lacking self-advocacy: Not clearly communicating your needs or asking for help. *Fix: Prepare for appointments and be clear about how arthritis affects your daily life.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While managing arthritis often involves day-to-day self-care, certain symptoms or changes warrant prompt medical advice. Catching potential issues early can prevent further complications and ensure your treatment plan remains effective.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't improve with rest.
  • New symptoms like fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss accompanying joint pain.
  • Rapid loss of function or mobility in a joint.
  • Side effects from medication that are concerning or severely impacting your daily life.
  • Your current treatment plan no longer seems to be managing your symptoms effectively.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can arthritis affect my ability to do my job?

Yes, arthritis can impact various aspects of your work, including physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. However, many people with arthritis work successfully, often with the help of adjustments and support.

What kind of "reasonable adjustments" can I ask for at work?

Reasonable adjustments are changes that help you do your job effectively. Examples include flexible working hours, ergonomic equipment (like a special chair or keyboard), adjusted duties, or even a change of workstation.

Do I have to tell my employer I have arthritis?

You are not legally obliged to disclose your arthritis unless it poses a health and safety risk. However, telling your employer can help them understand your needs and allow you to request reasonable adjustments.

Practical next steps for Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010

If you came here about Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Quick questions about Your Workplace Rights With

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
